summary:
Consensual same-sex relations became a criminal offence in Burkina Faso on 1 September 2025, when the Transitional Legislative Assembly passed the measure unanimously and it took effect on passage. The penalty is two to five years' imprisonment plus a fine. The criminal code in force from that date also prohibits the promotion of homosexuality or similar behaviour. Same-sex conduct had been lawful before, with an equal age of consent in place since 1996; the 2025 code ended that position.

The prohibition is carried by a revised Personal and Family Code that the junta's council of ministers approved by decree in July 2024, part of a junta-led overhaul of marriage and family law, and which entered into force on 1 September 2025 as criminal-code law. The vote was taken in an unelected 71-member transitional parliament. Military rule dates from September 2022.

Justice Minister Edasso Rodrigue Bayala has said the two-to-five-year terms and fines apply to perpetrators of "homosexual or similar practices", and that foreign nationals who violate the law will be deported. The offence is framed around acts rather than status, but a trans visitor whose relationship would be read locally as same-sex under birth-sex status falls within its terms, and removal from the country is the stated consequence for foreign nationals.

No arrests under the law had been reported as of 28 September 2025. Reporting by France 24 and AFP on 22 September 2025 described fear of a witch hunt and increased self-censorship within the LGBTQ community. The exposure a visitor faces is therefore statutory and discretionary rather than demonstrated through a record of prosecutions.

Article 23 of the Constitution defines marriage as the free consent of a man and a woman and describes the family as the basic unit of society owed state protection; it does not authorise same-sex marriage. Its anti-discrimination clause covers race, colour, religion, ethnicity, caste, social origin and wealth, and omits sexual orientation and gender identity. Pre-existing prohibitions on same-sex marriage and on adoption by same-sex couples remain in force. Under the adoption rules reported by the U.S. Department of State, only married, cohabiting heterosexual couples married at least five years may adopt, and single applicants are almost never permitted to adopt.

No mechanism for responding to anti-LGBT violence is documented. A 2011 human rights report found no legal discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation in employment, housing, statelessness, education or health care, while societal discrimination on those grounds persisted. LGBT people were reported as occasional victims of verbal and physical abuse; religious and traditional opinion did not accept homosexuality; and there were no reports that the government responded to societal violence or discrimination against them. LGBTQ organisations had no legal presence in the country, though they existed unofficially, with no reported violence against them. That assessment dates from 2011, before the criminalisation took effect.
tangentialFactors:
Burkina Faso joined roughly 22 of 54 African states that prohibit same-sex relations, according to the presidency's statement announcing the July 2024 decree. The count is a regional comparison, not a measure of enforcement intensity.

The law was enacted during a broader junta campaign against opposition parties, independent media and civil-society organisations, which is the context in which the transitional assembly voted. The same council of ministers approved the family code in July 2024.
localsOnly:
LGBTQ organisations have no legal presence in Burkina Faso; groups exist unofficially. The 2011 human rights report recorded no violence reported against those informal groups, and no government response to societal abuse or discrimination against LGBT people.

National adult HIV prevalence is 0.80% among people aged 15 to 49. Of an estimated 94,000 adults living with HIV, 65% receive antiretroviral drugs; 28% of children aged 0 to 14 do, against all-ages coverage of 32% in 2010. The figures describe the reach of the public treatment system, not any trans-specific service.

Marriage is constitutionally defined as the free consent of a man and a woman, and adoption is restricted to married, cohabiting heterosexual couples married at least five years, with single applicants almost never permitted. Neither route is open to a relationship the state reads as same-sex.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory records a prosecution, conviction or deportation under the September 2025 law after 28 September 2025; the enforcement record beyond that date is unresolved.

The inventory contains no information on legal gender recognition. No procedure, court order or administrative rule for changing name or gender markers on Burkinabé identity documents is described, and no rule on how a trans traveller's documents would be read at entry is available.

No trans-specific violence data and no general homicide rate for Burkina Faso appear in the inventory, so no comparison of trans-targeted violence against the background rate can be made.

The sources describe a July 2024 decree approving the Personal and Family Code and a 1 September 2025 vote in the transitional assembly without fully reconciling the sequence; the code's entry into force and the assembly vote are both dated 1 September 2025.

No information is available on police or border-screening practice toward gender-nonconforming travellers, nor on whether the promotion provision has been applied to online speech or media.
